Roman numeral analysis. Roman numeral analysis is the standard notational system for identifying chords and their harmonic functions within a tonal key. Using Roman numerals like I, IV, and V to denote chord scale degrees and uppercase and lowercase to indicate major and minor quality, it provides an elegant shorthand for understanding harmonic structure. Developed over centuries and codified in nineteenth-century theory pedagogy, roman numeral analysis remains the primary tool for musicians to comprehend how Classical, Baroque, and Romantic composers achieved coherence through harmonic logic. Capital Roman numerals like I, IV, and V denote major triads, while lowercase numerals like i, iv, and v denote minor triads in the same key position. In C major, I equals C major, IV equals F major, V equals G major. In C minor, i equals C minor, iv equals F minor, v equals G minor. The tonic chord, I, is the resting point. The dominant, V, creates tension. The subdominant, IV, bridges them—this hierarchy organizes entire pieces. Seventh chords add complexity. V7, the dominant seventh, is especially important, creating maximum tension resolved back to I. Figured bass, numbers beneath bass notes, is the historical precursor. Roman numerals evolved as a more explicit system for analysis. A progression like I-IV-V-I exemplifies the fundamental harmonic motion from stability through tension back to resolution. Extensions and modifications include secondary dominants like V of V, borrowed chords like iv in a major key, and chromatic alterations that complicate the basic system.
